summary:
FireScope is a web-based platform for exploring and comparing satellite active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments. Developed in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots," FireScope organizes historical observations into interactive maps, temporal calendars, and analytical views.

Rather than treating detections from different sensors as unique fire events, FireScope preserves sensor and platform identities to help users understand differences in satellite observations. Users can explore activity across geographic areas and time periods, compare MODIS and VIIRS records, and inspect sensor-specific Fire Radiative Power (FRP) measurements.

Built using NASA FIRMS data, FireScope emphasizes transparent data provenance, metric definitions, and scientific limitations. Its current historical archive focuses on Indonesia, providing a foundation for more comprehensive multi-sensor fire observation exploration and future validation.
details:
What does FireScope do?

FireScope is an interactive satellite active-fire observation platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, specifically the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots."

The platform helps users explore, compare, and analyze active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments across geographic regions and time periods. Instead of simply combining detection counts from different satellites, FireScope preserves sensor and satellite platform identities to provide a more transparent understanding of their observations.

Users can select an Area of Interest (AOI), explore historical and recent observations on an interactive map, inspect temporal activity through sensor-specific calendars, compare different periods and regions, and examine individual detection records, confidence information, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).How does it work?

FireScope combines several data sources and processing layers:

  • Historical observations: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS Collection 2 data are stored in Apache Parquet datasets and queried through DuckDB. The primary historical archive covers Indonesia from 2001 through November 2026.
  • Global reference data: Selected global fire-regime regions are supported by NASA FIRMS Area API archive observations covering specific historical periods. Additional recent global observations are obtained through live NASA FIRMS 24-hour feeds.
  • Multi-sensor analysis: MODIS Terra/Aqua and VIIRS Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 are analyzed separately. FireScope also provides constellation-aware per-satellite rates to help users understand how changes in the number of operational satellite platforms affect detection-count comparisons.
  • Spatiotemporal comparison: A co-location analysis groups spatially and temporally adjacent MODIS and VIIRS observations to distinguish cross-sensor co-detections from sensor-specific detections. These clusters represent analytical groupings, not independently confirmed fire incidents.
  • Interactive exploration: Processed data is exposed through an API and presented in an interactive workspace featuring geographic maps, time-series charts, activity calendars, regional comparisons, and detailed observation inspection.

Live NASA FIRMS observations and historical archive records are handled as distinct data sources with explicit time boundaries and provenance. Historical global coverage is not uniform: Indonesia has a multi-decade archive, while other regions have selected reference periods and live observations.

Benefits and intended impact

FireScope aims to make multi-sensor satellite fire observations easier to explore and interpret. It helps users identify temporal patterns, compare satellite platforms, investigate regional differences, and understand where sensor observations agree or differ.

By retaining native confidence information, reporting FRP in its original unit of megawatts (MW), exposing data provenance, and distinguishing unavailable data from periods with no recorded detections, FireScope encourages more responsible interpretation of satellite observations.

Our intended impact is to provide researchers, environmental analysts, and other users with a transparent exploration tool that can support wildfire observation analysis, regional comparisons, and further research into multi-sensor data harmonization. FireScope is designed as an analytical and exploratory platform, not as a replacement for ground verification or an authoritative fire-perimeter monitoring system.

Creativity and scientific considerations

Our approach focuses on making differences between satellite observations visible rather than hiding them behind a single combined number.

We consider differences in sensor spatial resolution, satellite acquisition opportunities, changing constellation sizes, native confidence scales, FRP measurements, temporal coverage, and data-processing status.

FireScope includes an experimental M3 empirical cross-sensor bridge that remains disabled by default. We also deliberately avoid unsupported cloud-coverage estimates or observation-probability gap filling because the available FIRMS feeds do not provide all the required satellite swath and cloud-mask information.

This emphasis on transparent methodology and explicit limitations is central to our approach: users should understand not only what the data shows, but also what it cannot establish.

Tools and technologies

FireScope was developed using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Leaflet, Express, DuckDB, Apache Parquet, and Bun.

Our primary data sources include NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1, NASA FIRMS VIIRS Collection 2, NASA FIRMS Area API, and NASA EONET v3 as a separate wildfire-event context source.

The application uses web-based mapping, data-processing, analytical, and visualization technologies to transform satellite observations into an interactive exploration experience.
